pages.name: The coin in the tank
pages.task: A coin lies in a tank of water. You push a rod straight at where it looks. The rod misses. Where is the coin really?
pages.why: Light from the coin bends as it leaves the water. Your eye traces it straight back, to a point above the real coin. So the coin is deeper than it looks.

Light from the coin bends at the surface on its way to the eye. Traced straight back, it seems to come from a point above the coin.
options: Nearer the surface than it looks
Off to one side, at the depth it looks

pages.name: Slower means a bend
pages.text: A ray meets water at 40° to the normal and carries on at 28.8°. Each end of its row of marchers slows as it crosses. So the row turns towards the normal. A faint ray reflects at 40°.

pages.name: Square on
pages.task: A ray strikes the water square on, along the normal. What does it do?
pages.why: Both ends of the marchers' row reach the water at the same moment. They slow together, so the row does not turn. The light still slows.

pages.name: The index
pages.text: Glass is given an index of 1.50 here. It slows light more than water does. So it bends the ray further towards the normal.

pages.name: Find the index
pages.task: Light travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in empty space and 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a glass block. What is the glass's refractive index?
pages.why: 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 2.00 × 10⁸ = 1.50. An index has no unit. It is one speed divided by another.

pages.name: Snell's law
pages.text: As the ray turns, both angles change. But sin i ÷ sin r stays at 1.333 for water. At 40°, the ray carries on at 28.8°.

pages.name: A water prism
pages.task: A glass prism with a 45° corner can turn light through 90°. Inside, the light meets the long face at 45°, and all of it reflects. Would a thin-walled prism filled with water do the same?
pages.answer: No, 45° is under water's critical angle
pages.why: Glass's critical angle is 41.8°, under 45°. So in glass the light reflects completely. Water's is 48.6°, more than 45°. So at 45° much of the light gets out through the long face. Two glass prisms can stand in for a periscope's two mirrors. Binoculars fold their light with prisms in the same way.
